slides.title: Clickjacking
slides.summary: An attacker loads your site in an invisible iframe and tricks the user into clicking your buttons.
body: Clickjacking (UI redressing) loads your page in a transparent iframe on the attacker's site, positioned over a decoy button. The user thinks they're clicking “Play video” but actually clicks “Delete account” or “Approve payment” on your site, while logged in.
<mark>If your site can be framed by anyone, any one-click action is at risk.</mark>
The fix is to tell the browser who may frame you:

ul: Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'none': nobody may frame this page.
X-Frame-Options: DENY: the older header. Keep it for old browsers; frame-ancestors wins where supported.

body.note: JavaScript “frame-busting” code is unreliable and can be blocked by the framing page. Use the headers.

steps.caption: The attacker's page shows a tempting button.
Your page sits on top, invisible, with “Transfer” over the decoy.
The user clicks; your site sees a genuine click from a real session.

item.label: Fix: frame-ancestors 'none'
item.sub: The browser refuses to render you in the frame

steps.caption: With the header, the iframe stays blank and nothing can be clicked.

slides.title: Embedding other sites safely
slides.summary: When you frame someone else's content, sandbox it and give it only the permissions it needs.
body: The other direction matters too. Widgets, ads, previews and user-supplied embeds run code you don't control.

ul: sandbox with no value blocks scripts, forms, popups, top navigation and same-origin access. Add back only what's needed, e.g. sandbox="allow-scripts".
Never combine allow-scripts and allow-same-origin for same-origin content: the frame can then remove its own sandbox.
allow grants powerful features (camera, payment, fullscreen) per frame.
referrerpolicy and loading="lazy" limit what leaks and when it loads.

body: <mark>Treat any iframe as untrusted: start from a full sandbox and add permissions one at a time.</mark>

slides.title: Talking to iframes with postMessage
slides.summary: postMessage crosses origins safely only if both sides check who they're talking to.
body: window.postMessage is the safe way to talk across origins, but it's a common source of DOM XSS when origins aren't checked.

ul: Sending: always pass an exact targetOrigin, never '*' for sensitive data.
Receiving: check event.origin against an allowlist before using event.data.
Validate the data like any other input. Never pass it to innerHTML or eval.

body: <mark>A message listener with no origin check accepts data from every site that can open or frame your page.</mark>
